newsitem.title: USA: GAO urges cuts in industrial bond volume caps.
newsitem.headline: GAO urges cuts in industrial bond volume caps.

text.p: The General Accounting Office has told the U.S. Congress that one way to help reduce the nation's deficit is to lower the volume cap on issuance of private activity bonds.
Private activity bonds are issued by state and local governments who provide the proceeds to private companies to finance, among other things, new or expanded manufacturing facilities.
Such private activity bonds are commonly refered to as industrial development bonds (IDBs).
IDB supporters say the bonds achieve public benefits like creating jobs, aiding poor neighborhoods, assisting start-up companies and keeping manufacturing firms in the U.S., GAO said.
But GAO said "there is no clear consensus on whether the bonds (really) achieve public benefits."
GAO noted that the Tax Reform Act of 1986 imposed a limit, or volume cap, that resricts the amount of bonds a state may issue to the greater of $50 per state resident or $150 million.
GAO offered three ways that Congress could reduce the tax losses associated with IDBs.
Congress could target cuts so that states with the fewest concentrations of the poor communities would face the deepest reductions, GAO said.
Congress also could simply reduce the cap proportionally across all states, GAO said.

"The 1995 cap was allocated to all states in such a way as to ensure a minimum of $150 million," GAO said. "Many states received more than $150 million, however, no states received less than this amount," GAO added.
"If the minimum allocation were reduced by $50 million and proportionally reduced in all states that received more than $150 million, the total cap would be reduced by 48 percent," GAO said.

Still another approach, GAO said, would be to both reduce the cap proportionally across all states and to target additional cuts to states with low concentration of poor localities. That approach would yield a 56 percent reduction in the caps, GAO said.
The recommendations were among 147 options floated by GAO on how Congress could reduce the federal deficit. The report is entitled "Addressing the Deficit" (B-274810).
